name: Glute bridges / glute activation

card.summary: A hip-lift exercise used to strengthen the glutes and, in posture circles, to counter anterior pelvic tilt; evidence for that use is absent.
card.note: Muscle-activation research exists; pelvic tilt and appearance outcomes are untested.

quick.overview:
Lying on the back with bent knees, the person lifts the hips by squeezing the glutes. It is a staple of posture routines aimed at anterior pelvic tilt.

Wikipedia lists it among suggested exercises but flags the sourcing as weak. No trial tests it for pelvic tilt or looks.
quick.mechanism: The glutes extend the hip. Proponents say strengthening them helps hold the pelvis in a more neutral position.
quick.risks: No specific harms are documented for bodyweight bridges. Back or hip pain is typically referred to a clinician.

lead: The glute bridge is a floor exercise in which a person lies on their back with knees bent and lifts the hips by contracting the gluteal and hamstring muscles. Related bridge exercises are described by Wikipedia as intended to improve lower back and gluteus strength [1]. People use it to build and wake up the glutes, which form the prominence of the buttocks and are widely seen as part of an athletic, well-proportioned physique [4].

The term glute activation refers to low-load drills such as bridges, clamshells and banded walks done before heavier training to switch on the gluteal muscles. T Nation training logs show lifters using single-leg glute bridges in warm-ups and as a way to find out whether the glutes are working [5][6].

In looksmaxxing and posture communities the glute bridge is also listed as a counter to anterior pelvic tilt, on the idea that weak glutes allow the pelvis to tip forward, giving a more upright stance and a flatter-looking lower back. Wikipedia's article on pelvic tilt lists glute bridges among recommended exercises, but flags that part of the article as relying on a consumer-health source [2].

chain: Hips lifted against gravity using glutes and hamstrings
Fuller glute shape and, per posture advocates, a more neutral pelvis and upright stance
angle.text: The glute bridge is used to strengthen and activate the muscle that shapes the buttocks and extends the hip, and is paired with hip flexor stretching in posture routines aimed at reducing anterior pelvic tilt.

infobox: Anterior pelvic tilt correction, couch stretch

paras: Bridge exercises are described as engaging the lower back, gluteus muscles and hips, along with the hamstrings and quadriceps. Common variants include a static hold and single-leg versions that increase the load on the hamstrings and glutes. The related gymnastic bridge is a distinct, more demanding movement [1].

The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the body and the main hip extender; Wikipedia lists hip thrusts, glute bridges, squats, deadlifts, kettlebell swings and lunges as exercises that target it, and notes that squats produce high levels of gluteal activation [4].
The gluteus maximus forms the prominence of the buttocks, and Wikipedia notes that strong, well-developed glutes are often seen as healthy and aesthetically appealing [4].

Posture sources describe the pelvic tilt pattern as hip flexors shortening while hip extensors, including the glutes, lengthen. Strengthening the glutes is therefore commonly paired with hip flexor stretching and core work [2][3]. Wikipedia notes that exercise recommendations in these articles are thinly referenced [2][3].

On T Nation, lifters describe using glute bridges to test glute engagement. One member advised another who could not feel the glutes working to try sets of bridges, with single-leg versions if strong enough, while noting that single-leg work made the other's hamstrings cramp [5]. Another member reported that a chiropractor found a weak, non-firing left glute and that repeated short sets across the day made a large difference [7]. Glute activation drills such as banded walks, clamshells and single-leg bridges also appear in lifters' warm-up routines [6][8].

Wikipedia cites a 2016 study in the Journal of Physical Therapy Science on trunk and hip extensor muscle activity during bridge exercises with varied unilateral knee angles, but its findings are not reported there [1]. That research concerns muscle activation, not pelvic alignment or appearance.
No studies found on glute bridges as a pelvic tilt or appearance intervention. Related laboratory work on muscle activity during bridge variations exists but did not measure those outcomes [1].
